candidates.speaker: Alex Malpass
candidates.proposition: The parity objection rules out temporally asymmetric models unless an independent symmetry breaker is supplied, while leaving symmetric finite-finite and infinite-infinite models open.
candidates.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly hands the discussion to Malpass, and the first-person explanation consistently states his own modal position.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This develops the central parity objection by specifying which temporal models survive and identifying the missing symmetry breaker required by Craig's position.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Craig's claim that parity between beginningless pasts and endless futures imposes an exceptionally radical modal burden on the objector.

candidates.contextSummary: After Craig presses the alleged burden of denying a beginning-without-end world, Malpass reframes the consequence as exclusion of asymmetric temporal structures rather than denial of every infinite temporal model.

candidates.speaker: William Lane Craig
candidates.proposition: A tensed theory supplies the relevant past-future asymmetry because future events do not yet exist and an endless future remains only potentially infinite, whereas a beginningless past cannot be potentially infinite in the same way.
candidates.attributionBasis: Craig announces what a defender of the argument will say and develops the view in first-person terms as his own tensed theory of time.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This is Craig's principal answer to the parity objection and is necessary to reconcile his rejection of an infinite past with acceptance of an endless future.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Malpass's contention that, without a symmetry breaker, past and future must have matching finite or infinite modal structures.

candidates.contextSummary: Craig distinguishes an endless but always finite future from a beginningless past by appealing to objective temporal becoming and the absence of presently existing future events.

candidates.speaker: William Lane Craig
candidates.proposition: Past events can instantiate an actual infinite despite no longer existing because they have occurred in reality, whereas future events have never been instantiated and remain unreal on a tensed theory.
candidates.attributionBasis: The response directly follows a question to Craig and uses his established terminology about instantiation, temporal becoming, and tensed time.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The distinction supplies the metaphysical basis for treating past and future differently and therefore underwrites Craig's response to the temporal parity objection.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: The objection that presentism makes both past and future events nonexistent now, apparently restoring symmetry between the two directions.

candidates.contextSummary: Craig contrasts tensed and tenseless theories, conceding parity on a tenseless view but arguing that objective temporal becoming makes an endless future finite at every stage.

candidates.speaker: Alex Malpass
candidates.proposition: Presentism does not break temporal symmetry because past events no longer exist while future events will exist, and Craig's potential-infinity argument equivocates between simple future and future-perfect claims.
candidates.attributionBasis: Malpass explicitly identifies himself as disagreeing with Craig and gives an extended first-person analysis using tense logic and his marble illustration.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This directly attacks the proposed symmetry breaker and argues that the tense distinction supporting Craig's treatment of an endless future is linguistically and logically unstable.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Craig's argument that objective temporal becoming distinguishes instantiated past events from unreal future events and makes only the future potentially infinite.

candidates.contextSummary: Malpass argues that correctly matching past, future, and future-perfect tenses restores symmetry, illustrating the point with marbles added daily to a jar over an endless future.

candidates.speaker: William Lane Craig
candidates.proposition: Even if actual infinite collections are possible, the past cannot be actually infinite because an actual infinite cannot be formed through the successive addition by which temporal events accumulate.
candidates.attributionBasis: The moderator expressly invites Craig to present his second philosophical argument, which Craig then states formally and illustrates at length.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This is the debate's second principal Kalam argument and directly supports the claim that the temporal past must be finite independently of objections to actual infinite collections.
candidates.contextSummary: Craig states a two-premise successive-addition argument, then supports it with the Jupiter-Saturn orbit comparison and a Grim Reaper construction said to yield contradiction.

candidates.speaker: Alex Malpass
candidates.proposition: The Jupiter-Saturn result reflects the ordinary cardinal behavior of infinite sets, while the real successive-addition issue is only that counting cannot reach a number lacking an immediate predecessor.
candidates.attributionBasis: The moderator gives Malpass the floor, and Malpass expressly evaluates Craig's planetary example before developing his own counting thought experiment.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The response separates familiar infinite-cardinality behavior from the transition question and narrows what the impossibility of counting to infinity can legitimately establish about time.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Craig's successive-addition argument and its claim that the planetary-orbit illustration exposes absurdity in a beginningless accumulated past.

candidates.contextSummary: Malpass accepts that time cannot contain moments more than finitely distant from one another but argues that endless counting still covers every natural number in the relevant cardinal sense.

candidates.speaker: William Lane Craig
candidates.proposition: From the fact that an endless counter can count every particular natural number, it does not follow that he will count all natural numbers, because that inference shifts modal or quantifier scope and commits composition.
candidates.attributionBasis: Craig addresses Malpass by name, labels the inference a modal-operator fallacy, and develops the criticism through explicit every-versus-all distinctions.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This challenges the key inference in Malpass's endless-counting reply and preserves the successive-addition argument by distinguishing distributive reachability from collective completion.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Malpass's claim that an endless counter's ability to count each natural number supports saying that the counter counts the entire infinite collection.

candidates.contextSummary: Craig uses counting, traversal, and composition examples to argue that each member's finite accessibility cannot establish that the whole infinite series is successively traversable.

candidates.speaker: Alex Malpass
candidates.proposition: Showing that every-to-all inferences sometimes fail does not show failure in the endless-counting case, where counting each natural number appears to make counting all of them a truth-preserving conclusion.
candidates.attributionBasis: Malpass resumes in first person, reconstructs Craig's objection with alternative examples, and repeatedly asks why that pattern fails in his actual counting case.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The reply contests whether Craig has diagnosed any fallacy in the specific inference under dispute and thus keeps the cardinal endless-counting objection alive.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Craig's assertion that moving from the ability to count every particular number to counting all numbers is a scope or composition fallacy.

candidates.contextSummary: Malpass contrasts invalid naming and motherhood examples with potentially valid whole-loaf reasoning, then argues that uninterrupted endless counting resembles the latter rather than the former.

candidates.speaker: William Lane Craig
candidates.proposition: Successive counting can never convert a potential infinite into an actual infinite, as Tristram Shandy can leave no particular page unwritten without ever completing the entire autobiography.
candidates.attributionBasis: Craig directly answers Malpass and invokes his standard potential-versus-actual infinite distinction together with the Tristram Shandy illustration.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This supplies a concrete countermodel to Malpass's claimed every-to-all inference and restates the mechanism at the heart of the successive-addition argument.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Malpass's insistence that, in uninterrupted endless counting, counting every natural number makes it legitimate to say that all natural numbers are counted.

candidates.contextSummary: Craig argues that infinite sets must be given tenselessly rather than generated temporally, illustrating the distinction through an autobiography with every page eventually written but never completed.

candidates.speaker: Alex Malpass
candidates.proposition: Craig's appeal to potential infinity relies on future-perfect claims about how many numbers will have been counted, which does not settle the distinct simple-future claim that every number will be counted.
candidates.attributionBasis: Malpass explicitly says the disagreement returns to tense and provides a sustained first-person distinction between simple-future and future-perfect formulations.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The tense distinction targets the logical form of Craig's Tristram Shandy response and offers a direct explanation of why finite completion at every stage need not defeat endless coverage.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Craig's claim that successive addition only yields a potential infinite and that Tristram Shandy can address every page without completing all pages.

candidates.contextSummary: Malpass explains future-perfect tense through a drinking example, concedes that no stage contains a completed infinity, and argues that Craig illegitimately transfers that result to simple-future claims.
